Latest resultsTest history Test explanations

Repository test report

This project presents a disk to an application and stores its data in a backing file. These tests check the engine, the applications that use it, and the tools used to verify the results. A passing test can mean a checker detected a deliberately wrong answer. Some test-program entries are child-process helpers; they are listed for inventory completeness, not as separate storage guarantees. The inventory includes executable tests and manual qualification procedures. It does not count builds, lint, setup checks, benchmarks, third-party tests, or proposals as correctness tests.

Test explanations

Backing fault scenarios

CHECK-05: Can both saved starting points still lead to valid data?

Setup
Two saved disk images came from real device tests in which the client flushed known bytes. One failed to write the record identifying a new checkpoint (a saved recovery starting point). The other wrote the record but failed its final sync.
Action or fault
The offline checker injects no new fault. Before engine recovery changes either image, it follows both checkpoint slots, processes later log records and checks the data blocks those records identify.
Expected outcome
Both starting points in each image must pass the checker’s bounds, reference and content checks. Testing only the newest slot could miss damage in the alternative starting point. This audit does not establish power-loss durability.
Earlier fault investigation · 19–20 Nov 2026

These are historical notes from the fault campaign, not observations from the repository run. Only the dated observations below give a verdict for this test run.

Expected. Both starting points in each image must pass the checker’s bounds, reference and content checks. Testing only the newest slot could miss damage in the alternative starting point. This audit does not establish power-loss durability.

Recorded result. The checker accepted both checkpoints in each image. .

CLOSE-01: Does normal close save a checkpoint without changing client data?

Setup
The test calls the engine directly, without a block-device client. It fills block 1 with 0x17, block 5 with 0x53, then block 1 again with 0xab. A flush confirms that the engine has made the writes persistent. On close the engine tries to save a new checkpoint, a starting point for recovery. It writes the record identifying that checkpoint into one of two reserved locations, leaving the older record intact.
Action or fault
No fault is injected. The engine uses a regular file exported by QEMU, the same backing path used to test write errors.
Expected outcome
Close must succeed. Only the alternate descriptor slot should change. Read a copy after close: block 1 must contain 0xab, block 5 must contain 0x53, and the other six blocks must still read as zero.
Earlier fault investigation · 19–20 Nov 2026

These are historical notes from the fault campaign, not observations from the repository run. Only the dated observations below give a verdict for this test run.

CLOSE-01: Does normal close save a checkpoint without changing client data?

Setup. The test calls the engine directly, without a block-device client. It fills block 1 with 0x17, block 5 with 0x53, then block 1 again with 0xab. A flush confirms that the engine has made the writes persistent. On close the engine tries to save a new checkpoint, a starting point for recovery. It writes the record identifying that checkpoint into one of two reserved locations, leaving the older record intact.

Fault or control. No fault is injected. The engine uses a regular file exported by QEMU, the same backing path used to test write errors.

Expected. Close must succeed. Only the alternate descriptor slot should change. Read a copy after close: block 1 must contain 0xab, block 5 must contain 0x53, and the other six blocks must still read as zero.

Recorded result. The original descriptor stayed unchanged, the alternate descriptor changed, and all eight blocks matched on a recovery copy. .

CLOSE-02: Does close report a failed checkpoint write even after client data was flushed?

Setup
The test calls the engine directly, without a block-device client. It fills block 1 with 0x17, block 5 with 0x53, then block 1 again with 0xab. A flush confirms that the engine has made the writes persistent. On close the engine tries to save a new checkpoint, a starting point for recovery. It writes the record identifying that checkpoint into one of two reserved locations, leaving the older record intact.
Action or fault
QEMU rejects the 4096-byte write at byte offset 4096 (sector 8) once. This is the new checkpoint descriptor, not one of the earlier client writes.
Expected outcome
The earlier flush must succeed, but close must report EIO (input/output error). Neither descriptor slot should change. Read a copy after close: block 1 must contain 0xab, block 5 must contain 0x53, and the other six blocks must still read as zero.
Earlier fault investigation · 19–20 Nov 2026

These are historical notes from the fault campaign, not observations from the repository run. Only the dated observations below give a verdict for this test run.

CLOSE-02: Does close report a failed checkpoint write even after client data was flushed?

Setup. The test calls the engine directly, without a block-device client. It fills block 1 with 0x17, block 5 with 0x53, then block 1 again with 0xab. A flush confirms that the engine has made the writes persistent. On close the engine tries to save a new checkpoint, a starting point for recovery. It writes the record identifying that checkpoint into one of two reserved locations, leaving the older record intact.

Fault or control. QEMU rejects the 4096-byte write at byte offset 4096 (sector 8) once. This is the new checkpoint descriptor, not one of the earlier client writes.

Expected. The earlier flush must succeed, but close must report EIO (input/output error). Neither descriptor slot should change. Read a copy after close: block 1 must contain 0xab, block 5 must contain 0x53, and the other six blocks must still read as zero.

Recorded result. Close returned EIO. Both descriptors were unchanged and all eight recovered blocks matched. A close error did not cancel the earlier successful flush. .

CLOSE-03: Can the close test distinguish a genuine write error from a missed injection?

Setup
The test calls the engine directly, without a block-device client. It fills block 1 with 0x17, block 5 with 0x53, then block 1 again with 0xab. A flush confirms that the engine has made the writes persistent. On close the engine tries to save a new checkpoint, a starting point for recovery. It writes the record identifying that checkpoint into one of two reserved locations, leaving the older record intact.
Action or fault
The checker expects the close-time descriptor write to fail. The test deliberately aims QEMU’s rule at sector 3000 instead of sector 8, so it does not reject that write.
Expected outcome
Close should succeed. The checker must then fail because the expected input/output error did not occur. Otherwise a broken setup could be counted as evidence that the engine handles faults.
Earlier fault investigation · 19–20 Nov 2026

These are historical notes from the fault campaign, not observations from the repository run. Only the dated observations below give a verdict for this test run.

CLOSE-03: Can the close test distinguish a genuine write error from a missed injection?

Setup. The test calls the engine directly, without a block-device client. It fills block 1 with 0x17, block 5 with 0x53, then block 1 again with 0xab. A flush confirms that the engine has made the writes persistent. On close the engine tries to save a new checkpoint, a starting point for recovery. It writes the record identifying that checkpoint into one of two reserved locations, leaving the older record intact.

Fault or control. The checker expects the close-time descriptor write to fail. The test deliberately aims QEMU’s rule at sector 3000 instead of sector 8, so it does not reject that write.

Expected. Close should succeed. The checker must then fail because the expected input/output error did not occur. Otherwise a broken setup could be counted as evidence that the engine handles faults.

Recorded result. The checker reported “checkpoint close missed EIO”. This is a successful control of the checker, not a successful recovery from a fault. .

Can someone reproduce the same fault run without the generator?

Setup
Run seed 42 twice on separate fresh files. For a third fresh run, read the saved list of writes, faults and target operations instead of drawing any random numbers.
Action or fault
The plan rejects the second sync in the first round. In later rounds it rejects the third write for lack of space, completes zero bytes on the third write, and rejects the second write for lack of space. Each round opens a recovered copy before the next round starts.
Expected outcome
The client errors, fault hits, recovered block values and final verdict must match in all three runs. Compare both the plan files and trace files byte for byte. Matching pass labels alone would not prove that the runs took the same path.
Earlier fault investigation · 19–20 Nov 2026

These are historical notes from the fault campaign, not observations from the repository run. Only the dated observations below give a verdict for this test run.

Can someone reproduce the same fault run without the generator?

Setup. Run seed 42 twice on separate fresh files. For a third fresh run, read the saved list of writes, faults and target operations instead of drawing any random numbers.

Fault or control. The plan rejects the second sync in the first round. In later rounds it rejects the third write for lack of space, completes zero bytes on the third write, and rejects the second write for lack of space. Each round opens a recovered copy before the next round starts.

Expected. The client errors, fault hits, recovered block values and final verdict must match in all three runs. Compare both the plan files and trace files byte for byte. Matching pass labels alone would not prove that the runs took the same path.

Observed. All comparisons passed. This demonstrates repeatable serialized operations, not repeatable kernel thread scheduling.

Can the engine recover after faults chosen by a seed?

Setup
A seed is a number used to generate the same schedule on demand. On a fresh file the client writes and flushes a known block. It then follows four rounds of generated writes to numbered blocks; after each successful write it requests a flush. The default engine has retry disabled.
Action or fault
Each round targets one numbered backing write or sync. The five possible effects are: refuse a write for lack of space, complete zero bytes instead of a full write, report an error after a write actually completes, refuse a sync, or report an error after a sync actually completes. The cut used here retains completed writes; it does not simulate power loss.
Expected outcome
Check that the scheduled fault fired once and the client received the specified error. Another flush must fail. Open a copy taken before shutdown and compare all eight blocks with a separate history of the bytes that should have reached this file. Continue from that recovered copy.
Earlier fault investigation · 19–20 Nov 2026

These are historical notes from the fault campaign, not observations from the repository run. Only the dated observations below give a verdict for this test run.

REOPEN-03: What if neither half of an overwrite reaches disk?

Setup
The client fills block 0 with the byte 0x11 and block 1 with 0x22, then flushes both writes to storage. It overwrites block 1 with 0x33 without another flush. On disk, that overwrite adds two pieces: 4 KiB of new data and a 4 KiB footer that identifies block 1 and gives the checksum for its new data.
Action or fault
The test builds a disk copy from before the overwrite. It keeps neither the new data nor its footer. No running-device error is injected.
Expected outcome
Reopening the copy must leave the earlier write visible: every byte of block 1 should still be 0x22. The overwrite was never flushed, so the absence of the whole new record is a permitted outcome.

Setup
The client fills block 0 with the byte 0x11 and block 1 with 0x22, then flushes both writes to storage. It overwrites block 1 with 0x33 without another flush. The client fills block 0 with the byte 0x11 and block 1 with 0x22, then flushes both writes to storage. It overwrites block 1 with 0x33 without another flush. UBLK-01: Can an ordinary write make room without losing flushed data?

Setup
A client writes through a real Linux block device served by the engine. It fills block 1 with 0x17, block 5 with 0x53, and block 1 again with 0xab. It then asks the engine to flush, or make those writes persistent. The flush confirms the latest values: every byte of block 1 is 0xab and every byte of block 5 is 0x53. The six unwritten blocks read as zero. Repeated writes of 0x53 to block 5 make the engine run out of immediately usable space.
Action or fault
To make room, the engine saves a checkpoint: a record of where data lives and which disk regions can be reused. This checkpoint, called B in the trace, can release six regions. Its descriptor is the small record that tells recovery where to find it. No fault is injected. The test switches the backing path at the checkpoint boundary, as it does in the error cases, but leaves the error rule off.
Expected outcome
The waiting write should succeed. Only after the checkpoint finishes may the engine reuse the old space. Reopening a copy should return the flushed contents. Without this control, damage caused by the test setup could look like an engine fault.
Earlier fault investigation · 19–20 Nov 2026

These are historical notes from the fault campaign, not observations from the repository run. Only the dated observations below give a verdict for this test run.

The test switches the backing path at the checkpoint boundary, as it does in the error cases, but leaves the error rule off.

Recorded result. The write completed all 4096 bytes. The engine freed six regions and sent four requests to discard underlying storage. All eight logical blocks matched after reopen. .

Setup. This tests the simulator itself. Try an empty image, invalid fault rules and a discard past the end of a two-byte disk.

Fault or control. Examples include a supposedly short write that completes the full count, an address change on a sync that has no address, an out-of-bounds destination and call number zero. Separately issue 32 valid syncs and then request one more.

Expected. Reject each invalid input and the extra sync with a validation error. A malformed or over-budget run is not evidence of storage failure or success.

Recorded result. Passed in the Python model tests; this is not a live-device fault result. .

Stop checking rather than silently guessing when the input is invalid or too large

Setup
The history checker normally records one value per simulated block. Feed it invalid events: an unsupported operation or outcome, an invalid block number, a discard carrying data, a write of the wrong width, and a flush with a block address.
Action or fault
Then start nine blocks at the character 0 and report a write of X with an unknown outcome to each. Each affected block might hold either value, so the number of combinations doubles per write.
Expected outcome
Reject each invalid event. Reject the ninth uncertain write when it exceeds the limit of 256 possible states. Silently discarding possibilities would make the checker’s verdict unreliable.

Can a saved plan silently change meaning or request unsupported work?

Setup
Fault schedules can be saved and replayed; changing their text format could silently change the workload.
Action or fault

Expected outcome
Valid text must round-trip unchanged. Invalid schedules must be rejected before the engine runs.
Earlier fault investigation · 19–20 Nov 2026

These are historical notes from the fault campaign, not observations from the repository run. Only the dated observations below give a verdict for this test run.

Can a saved plan silently change meaning or request unsupported work?

Setup. Generate the version-1 plan for seed 42. Compare its exact text with a fixed reference, then read the reference back and write it out again. No engine, client writes or backing faults run in this test.

Fault or control. Change the input text: use an unknown fault, a zero occurrence number, an out-of-range block or byte, no writes, too many writes, too many rounds or an unsupported version.

Expected. The valid plan must match the reference and survive the text round trip unchanged. Every malformed example must be rejected. Otherwise the same saved schedule could acquire different effects or exceed the test’s bounds.

Observed. Passed: the reference and rejection checks succeeded. This tests plan generation and reading, not data recovery.

Can retry be enabled without exclusive access or enough memory?

Setup
Keeping replay copies requires both exclusive access to the backing file and space in the engine’s memory budget.
Action or fault
Try enabling retry with conflicting ownership, with too little memory, and when both requirements are met.
Expected outcome
The engine must refuse unsupported configurations and account for the extra memory within its budget when it succeeds.
Earlier fault investigation · 19–20 Nov 2026

These are historical notes from the fault campaign, not observations from the repository run. Only the dated observations below give a verdict for this test run.

Can retry be enabled without exclusive access or enough memory?

Setup. Open a temporary volume. A second file handle holds an exclusive lock on its backing file. In a separate check reopen the volume with a memory budget that covers its existing allocations but leaves no room for retained records.

Fault or control. No client writes, flushes or storage errors. The test changes two prerequisites for enabling library retry: lock availability and memory budget.

Expected. While the other handle holds the lock, enabling retry must report that it would block and leave the budget unchanged. After releasing the lock, enabling retry must succeed within budget. With too little memory it must reject the configuration. Otherwise replay could compete with a writer or exceed its stated memory limit.

Observed. Passed: the three enable attempts returned the expected lock refusal, success and budget refusal.

Earlier fault investigation · 19–20 Nov 2026

These are historical notes from the fault campaign, not observations from the repository run. Only the dated observations below give a verdict for this test run.

Can the checker distinguish repeatable results from repeatably wrong results?

Setup. Generate the four-round schedule for seed 42, write it as text, read it back and run both schedules on fresh volumes. The runner writes a known value to block 6 before the planned writes. It tracks expected block contents separately from the engine.

Fault or control. For a negative control, deliberately send that initial write to block 7 instead of block 6 without changing the expected history. For a second control, supply a plan with just one write and flush but target the second backing sync, which cannot occur.

Expected. The ordinary runs must pass with identical traces. The misdirected write must produce a mismatch at block 6 after reopen. The unreachable fault must be reported as a missed injection rather than as an engine pass.

Observed. Passed: the Rust test checked all three outcomes. It does not rely on the engine to supply its own expected bytes.

Can the engine restore the actual bytes before it reports a successful flush?

Setup
The client flushes two old values, then overwrites both blocks with library retry enabled before the writes.
Action or fault
Remove both new records from the backing file at flush and report an I/O error.
Expected outcome
The engine must rewrite the saved bytes at their original locations and sync before reporting success. Reopening a copy must return both new values.
Earlier fault investigation · 19–20 Nov 2026

These are historical notes from the fault campaign, not observations from the repository run. Only the dated observations below give a verdict for this test run.

Can the engine restore the actual bytes before it reports a successful flush?

Setup. Enable library retry on a temporary volume before the client writes. Flush old values in blocks 0 and 1, then overwrite both. The engine keeps an in-memory copy of each new physical record, including the block data and the information needed to locate and verify it.

Fault or control. At the next flush the test removes both new records from the backing file and reports one input/output error. The file is still the same file and subsequent writes can succeed.

Expected. The engine must rewrite both complete records at the same offsets in their original order, then sync. Only then may it return success to the client. A copy opened immediately afterwards must contain both new values.

Observed. Passed at 067fd12: two 8192-byte records were rewritten at offsets 28672 and 36864. The test compared all the bytes, not just a checksum. This checks the explicitly enabled library feature; the default daemon does not perform this retry.

Does a discard prevent replay of an obsolete write?

Setup
The engine has buffered enough information to replay recent writes but then receives a discard, which changes the valid data history.
Action or fault
Inject a sync failure at the next flush.
Expected outcome
Do not replay the pre-discard history: return the error after one sync attempt and stop serving requests on the volume.
Earlier fault investigation · 19–20 Nov 2026

These are historical notes from the fault campaign, not observations from the repository run. Only the dated observations below give a verdict for this test run.

Does a discard prevent replay of an obsolete write?

Setup. Enable library retry and flush once. Write block 0, then discard it: the client has told the engine that the old contents are no longer needed. A saved copy of the write alone cannot represent both operations.

Fault or control. Reject every subsequent backing sync with an input/output error. No bytes are deliberately erased by this injection.

Expected. The client flush must fail on the first sync error and the volume must stop. Retrying just the old write would risk bringing back data the client discarded.

Observed. Passed: the injector counted one sync attempt, not two, and the test observed the failed volume. The test checks refusal to retry; it does not claim to have observed discarded data reappear.

Recorded observations

Does retry apply a write twice when the original sync actually succeeded?

Setup
A volume with retry enabled writes a known block and records the current log sequence number.
Action or fault
Let the underlying sync succeed but report an error once. Flush again after writing a different block.
Expected outcome

Earlier fault investigation · 19–20 Nov 2026

These are historical notes from the fault campaign, not observations from the repository run. Only the dated observations below give a verdict for this test run.

Does retry apply a write twice when the original sync actually succeeded?

Setup. Enable library retry and complete an initial flush. Write block 0 with byte 0x31 throughout. Record the sequence number of the last log entry; a new logical update would advance it.

Fault or control. Let the backing sync finish successfully, then report one input/output error to the engine. No records are lost here. The engine cannot tell from the error alone that the original write is safe.

Expected. The client flush must succeed without advancing the log sequence number. To prove service resumed, write byte 0x32 to block 1, flush again, reopen the volume and check both complete blocks.

Observed. Passed: one injected error, unchanged log sequence number after retry, and both blocks matched after reopen.

Earlier fault investigation · 19–20 Nov 2026

These are historical notes from the fault campaign, not observations from the repository run. Only the dated observations below give a verdict for this test run.

Does the engine stop if restoring the writes still does not make them durable?

Setup. Enable library retry, complete an initial flush, then write block 0. The engine has a record it could rewrite if a sync fails.

Fault or control. Reject every subsequent request to sync the backing file with an input/output error. The injector refuses the sync before it runs; it does not erase written bytes.

Expected. The first sync fails. Even if the engine rewrites the record, the second sync must fail too. The client must get an error, the volume must enter its failed state and another client flush must not trigger more attempts.

Observed. Passed: two injected errors, one failed client flush and no further sync attempt on the next flush.

REOPEN-07: Can recovery use an older checkpoint without returning older data?

Setup
Two checkpoints provide alternative starting points for recovery. Valid records follow the older one.
Action or fault
Damage the descriptor that identifies the newer checkpoint, then reopen the volume.
Expected outcome
Start from the older usable checkpoint and apply the valid later records. The client must still read the expected values, not just the older checkpoint's state.
Earlier fault investigation · 19–20 Nov 2026

These are historical notes from the fault campaign, not observations from the repository run. Only the dated observations below give a verdict for this test run.

REOPEN-07: Can recovery use an older checkpoint without returning older data?

Setup. The engine has two saved starting points for recovery, called checkpoints. Each points to an index that lets the engine find earlier writes. The test writes known values and closes the volume twice to publish two checkpoints. It opens the volume again, overwrites all three logical blocks, flushes the writes and stops without publishing another checkpoint.

Fault or controlled change. The test corrupts one byte of the descriptor identifying the newest checkpoint. The older checkpoint and the later records of flushed writes remain intact.

Expected outcome. The engine must open using the older valid checkpoint and apply the subsequent writes in order. Choosing an older starting point does not authorize discarding later flushed writes. Blocks 0, 1 and 2 must return their latest byte patterns: 0xd4, 0xe7 and 0x7e respectively.

Recorded result. The test passed: the engine started from the older checkpoint, reached the last recorded write and returned all three expected blocks.

REOPEN-08: What if the newest checkpoint points to a damaged index?

Setup
The newest checkpoint points to a page that identifies saved mappings. An older checkpoint is still available.
Action or fault
Damage the newer checkpoint's index page without damaging the older one or the later valid log records.
Expected outcome
Reopen from the older checkpoint and recover the later updates. Falling back must not discard those client writes.
Earlier fault investigation · 19–20 Nov 2026

These are historical notes from the fault campaign, not observations from the repository run. Only the dated observations below give a verdict for this test run.

REOPEN-08: What if the newest checkpoint points to a damaged index?

Setup. The engine has two saved starting points for recovery, called checkpoints. Each points to an index that lets the engine find earlier writes. The test writes known values and closes the volume twice to publish two checkpoints. It opens the volume again, overwrites all three logical blocks, flushes the writes and stops without publishing another checkpoint.

Fault or controlled change. The newest checkpoint’s descriptor is intact. Instead the test changes one byte in the index page it points to. Trusting just the descriptor could leave recovery using damaged information about where the client’s data lives.

Expected outcome. Use the older checkpoint with an intact index, then apply the later writes. The client must get the last flushed byte pattern from each whole block: 0xd4 at block 0, 0xe7 at block 1 and 0x7e at block 2.

Recorded result. The test passed: the engine reopened from the older checkpoint and returned the expected bytes through the latest write.

REOPEN-09: What if neither checkpoint can start recovery?

Setup
A disk image has two possible starting points for recovery.
Action or fault
Corrupt the newer checkpoint descriptor and a page needed by the older checkpoint. Attempt to open the volume twice.
Expected outcome
Both attempts must return an invalid-data error, without a panic or any change to the damaged image.
Earlier fault investigation · 19–20 Nov 2026

These are historical notes from the fault campaign, not observations from the repository run. Only the dated observations below give a verdict for this test run.

REOPEN-09: What if neither checkpoint can start recovery?

Setup. The engine has two saved starting points for recovery, called checkpoints. Each points to an index that lets the engine find earlier writes. The test writes known values and closes the volume twice to publish two checkpoints. It opens the volume again, overwrites all three logical blocks, flushes the writes and stops without publishing another checkpoint.

Fault or controlled change. The test changes a byte in the newest checkpoint’s descriptor and a byte in an index page belonging to the older checkpoint. It saves a byte-for-byte copy of the damaged image before attempting to open it.

Expected outcome. With no usable checkpoint the engine must refuse to open the volume. Guessing where the latest data lives could return wrong bytes. Refusing to open must neither crash the process nor change the disk image; another open attempt must get the same result.

Recorded result. Both open attempts reported invalid data. After each refusal, the test compared the complete file to the saved damaged image and found no changes.

REOPEN-10: Can the engine tell an intact old record from a damaged new one?

Setup
A disk region is reused, leaving an intact record from its earlier use where recovery is looking for a new update.
Action or fault
Present the recovery scanner with the old record, then with damaged or misplaced versions.
Expected outcome
It should recognize intact stale data as the end of new updates, but reject the invalid versions. Old bytes must not authorize arbitrary corruption.
Earlier fault investigation · 19–20 Nov 2026

These are historical notes from the fault campaign, not observations from the repository run. Only the dated observations below give a verdict for this test run.

REOPEN-10: Can the engine tell an intact old record from a damaged new one?

Setup. Ordinary writes, discards, flushes and volume growth caused the engine to reuse disk space. After a clean close, one saved image had a current record numbered 83 in physical block 4. Block 5 still held a much older record numbered 3. Both uses of that region had placed a record after block 4, so the predecessor’s address alone could not tell recovery which write came next.

Fault or controlled change. No fault was injected in the original workload. To test the repair directly, a separate regression places a valid older record where recovery would look for the next one. It then tries a damaged header, a damaged checksum and an intact old record that identifies a different disk address.

Expected outcome. Recovery must not treat a valid leftover as a new update or refuse to open an otherwise valid volume. But an unreadable or misplaced record is not proof of harmless age: the regression must reject each damaged or misplaced case.

Recorded result. Before the repair, two workloads could not reopen a valid volume. After the repair, all six workload and cache combinations reopened and matched 680 logical blocks per test interval. The focused regression rejected damaged and misplaced records.

SEAM-05: Does a zero-byte overwrite replace a previously flushed block?

Setup
Block 2 already contains a flushed pattern.
Action or fault
Replace it while the backing write reports zero bytes transferred.
Expected outcome
The overwrite must fail and stop the volume. Count one error, no additional completed bytes and no pending work. After reopening, block 2 must still contain the original pattern.
Earlier fault investigation · 19–20 Nov 2026

These are historical notes from the fault campaign, not observations from the repository run. Only the dated observations below give a verdict for this test run.

SEAM-05: Does a zero-byte overwrite replace a previously flushed block?

Setup. The test writes 0x22 throughout logical block 2 and flushes it. It saves the backing bytes and the engine’s I/O counters, then tries to overwrite the same block with 0x33.

Fault or control. The hook makes the first backing write for the overwrite complete zero bytes. No overwrite bytes reach the file.

Expected. Fail the overwrite and stop serving requests. Count one error, no bytes written and no requests left pending. Reopen and read block 2: it must still contain 0x22. Counting an incomplete write as progress could hide the failure.

Recorded result. The engine rejected the overwrite and marked the volume failed. It counted one error, no additional bytes written, and no pending requests. The image did not change; after reopen, block 2 held the earlier value. .

Recorded observations

SEAM-06: Does the default engine stop after a sync reports failure even if bytes reached disk?

Setup
The client overwrites a previously flushed block.
Action or fault
Let the backing sync finish but make it report an error to the engine.
Expected outcome
The engine cannot assume success: the flush must fail and the volume must stop. On this particular image the new value must survive because the underlying sync actually finished.
Earlier fault investigation · 19–20 Nov 2026

These are historical notes from the fault campaign, not observations from the repository run. Only the dated observations below give a verdict for this test run.

SEAM-06: Does the default engine stop after a sync reports failure even if bytes reached disk?

Setup. The caller writes 0x55 throughout block 1 and successfully flushes it. It overwrites the same block with 0x66 and flushes again.

Fault or control. The test lets the second backing sync finish successfully, then reports EIO (input/output error) instead of success to the engine. The caller cannot tell from EIO whether the new bytes survived.

Expected. Report EIO to the caller and refuse a subsequent flush. In this specific test the sync really completed, so reopening must return 0x66. A failed call does not prove rollback.

Recorded result. The second flush returned EIO, the next flush returned “volume failed”, and block 1 contained 0x66 on reopen. .

Recorded observations

SEAM-07: Can the volume still be used after a write is refused before any storage I/O?

Setup
The engine has no room to admit another write.
Action or fault
Attempt a write with a backing-write error rule armed, then request a flush.
Expected outcome
The engine must report no space before reaching the rule. This refusal must not stop the volume: the next flush must succeed.
Earlier fault investigation · 19–20 Nov 2026

These are historical notes from the fault campaign, not observations from the repository run. Only the dated observations below give a verdict for this test run.

SEAM-07: Can the volume still be used after a write is refused before any storage I/O?

Setup. The test creates a small, five-region volume, writes and flushes block 0, then tries to write block 1. There is not enough usable space for that operation.

Fault or control. No backing error is intended. A trap would reject the next backing data write with EIO. Its count must remain zero, proving that the capacity check refused this write before submitting data.

Expected. Return ENOSPC (“no space left”) without changing the image or stopping the volume. A later flush must succeed because this refusal left no write with an uncertain outcome.

Recorded result. The trap recorded zero hits, the image was unchanged and the later flush succeeded. .

SEAM-08: Does a no-space error from storage stop the volume when a checkpoint may be incomplete?

Setup
Engine maintenance has written the record identifying a new checkpoint but still needs a final sync before releasing space.
Action or fault
Reject that sync for lack of space.
Expected outcome
The engine must keep the earlier checkpoint active, stop serving the volume and reject the next flush rather than reuse space whose release was never confirmed.
Earlier fault investigation · 19–20 Nov 2026

These are historical notes from the fault campaign, not observations from the repository run. Only the dated observations below give a verdict for this test run.

SEAM-08: Does a no-space error from storage stop the volume when a checkpoint may be incomplete?

Setup. The test writes blocks 0, 1 and 2 twice, then flushes. Maintenance saves a checkpoint that keeps a disk region reserved. The next checkpoint could make it reusable: maintenance syncs the records, writes the new checkpoint descriptor, then syncs that descriptor.

Fault or control. Reject the second sync in this maintenance call with ENOSPC (“no space left”). Unlike a refusal before any write, the descriptor has already been written. Its persistence is uncertain.

Expected. Return ENOSPC, keep the earlier checkpoint active in memory and refuse the next flush. A successful later flush would let the volume continue as if publication had completed safely.

Recorded result. Before the fix the next flush succeeded. After the fix the same fault fired once, the engine stopped the volume and the next flush failed. This case demonstrates an incorrect success before the fix, not observed data loss. .

Recorded observations

What if the buffer for saving replay copies fills up?

Setup
The memory reserved for replay copies is full. Accepting more writes would require dropping some retained bytes.
Action or fault
Submit the write that triggers an internal sync and make that sync fail.
Expected outcome
The write must fail and the engine must stop rather than evict bytes it would need to make earlier writes durable.
Earlier fault investigation · 19–20 Nov 2026

These are historical notes from the fault campaign, not observations from the repository run. Only the dated observations below give a verdict for this test run.

What if the buffer for saving replay copies fills up?

Setup. Enable library retry and complete an initial flush. Repeatedly overwrite block 0 without another client flush. Each write requires memory for a copy of the physical record. Eventually the engine must sync the earlier writes before it can use that memory for the next record.

Fault or control. Reject the first backing sync with an input/output error. The next client write triggers that internal sync because there is not enough space to retain another record. This is a memory limit, not a full disk.

Expected. The write must report the error and the volume must stop. Discarding the old copies and continuing would leave the engine unable to restore everything covered by an eventual client flush.

Observed. Passed: no sync fault fired during the initial sequence; the next write returned EIO, with one fault hit and the volume in its failed state.

Recorded observations

What if the first write happened before retry was enabled?

Setup
The engine accepts a write before the caller enables replay. Its retained copies therefore cover only part of the writes awaiting a flush.
Action or fault
Enable retry, add a write, then make the sync fail.
Expected outcome
Return an error after one sync attempt. Replaying only the retained subset must not turn the incomplete flush into a success.
Earlier fault investigation · 19–20 Nov 2026

These are historical notes from the fault campaign, not observations from the repository run. Only the dated observations below give a verdict for this test run.

What if the first write happened before retry was enabled?

Setup. Write block 0, enable library retry, then write block 1. There is no successful flush between these writes. A flush now covers both blocks, including the write made before retry was enabled.

Fault or control. Reject each backing sync with an input/output error. The injection blocks sync; it does not remove either record from the file.

Expected. Refuse the client flush and stop serving the volume after the first error. A partial list of writes cannot justify a promise that both blocks are durable.

Observed. Passed: exactly one sync error and a failed volume. There was no second sync attempt with an incomplete set of records.

Would the test catch a flush that succeeded without saving the writes?

Setup
Two controls start with flushed old values, then overwrite the same two blocks.
Action or fault
Run once without faults. In the broken control, drop both new records and report a successful flush after repeating only the sync.
Expected outcome
The clean copy must contain both new values. The checker must catch both old values in the broken copy; detecting false success is the passing outcome.
Earlier fault investigation · 19–20 Nov 2026

These are historical notes from the fault campaign, not observations from the repository run. Only the dated observations below give a verdict for this test run.

Would the test catch a flush that succeeded without saving the writes?

Setup. Two controls start from separate files. In each, the client flushes old values in blocks 0 and 1, overwrites both, and requests another flush. The test keeps the two expected new values outside the backing file.

Fault or control. The clean control injects nothing. In the broken control the test removes both new records, reports a sync error inside the test backing layer, then deliberately repeats only the sync. With no writes left to save, that second sync succeeds. The layer reports success to the engine.

Expected. Open a copy taken at client completion, before a clean shutdown can write anything else. Both new values must be present in the clean control. In the broken control the client saw success but both old values must be found instead. The test must detect the disagreement.

Observed. Both controls passed: the clean file contained the new values and the comparison rejected the false success. This proves the check can catch missing data; the bare retry is deliberately broken test code, not the engine’s repair.

Recorded observations
